title: Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows
author: Ava Thompson
summary: Comprehensive controlbook describing RBAC and authentication, audit logging standards and retention, data residency and retention policy, secure SDLC requirements, incident response security procedures, evidence collection workflows for audits, and the process for risk and exceptions.
content:
Purpose

This controlbook centralizes Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls for access, logging, data residency/retention, secure software development, incident response, and compliance evidence workflows. It is intended for engineers, product owners, security reviewers, and compliance auditors.

Scope

Applies to: all Redwood codebases, hosted and private deployments, control plane services, operator tooling, CI/CD pipelines, and customer-facing logs and telemetry. Does not replace customer-specific contractual obligations; it complements the compliance addenda in contracts.

Owners and Review Cadence

- Document owner: Security (security@redwood.example.com)
- Primary owners: Security Engineering (owner), Platform (co-owner), Eng Infra (co-owner)
- Review cadence: quarterly for controls, annually for retention schedules, ad-hoc for major platform changes or new regulatory requirements

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview
- Redwood uses centralized identity and access management (IAM) for both internal and customer-facing control planes. Internal access is managed through the corporate identity provider (IdP) with SCIM provisioning. Service-to-service auth uses short-lived mTLS certificates or workload identity where supported.

Role model (high level)
- system-admin: full administrative access to platform control plane and prod infra; requires 2FA + manager approval and quarterly access review.
- infra-operator: ability to deploy and manage infrastructure, view production metrics; scoped to specific AWS/GCP projects.
- svc-owner: access to a single service configuration, logs, and runbooks; used for on-call owners.
- developer: repository write + CI access for non-prod, limited prod ops via well-defined runbooks and ephemeral access requests.
- auditor: read-only access to audit logs and compliance dashboards; granted for audit windows.

Practical controls and requirements
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) enforced via role-based groups; no permanent account should have broad system-admin privileges.
- All privileged roles require 2FA (hardware key recommended) and JIT (just-in-time) ephemeral elevation for sensitive ops. Elevation must be approved via Slack + ticket system and logged.
- Service accounts: limited to required scopes; credentials rotated by automation every 7 days for high-privilege tokens, 90 days for lower-privilege service tokens. Secrets are stored in KMS-backed vaults; HSM-backed keys required for production key material.
- RBAC change process: changes must be requested via the access request workflow, include justification and owner, and be approved by the role steward. All changes produce an audit trail with requester, approver, TTL, and rationale.

Enforcement and detection
- Periodic access reviews: quarterly automated review for all system-admin and infra-operator groups; ad-hoc review after personnel changes.
- Misuse detection: alert on privilege escalation requests outside business hours or from anomalous IPs (configured in SIEM).

2) Audit Logging

Logging scope
- Capture: IAM events (logins, privilege changes), admin API calls, deployment actions, configuration changes, data access to sensitive stores (PII, customer data), and pipeline secrets access.
- Log transport: logs ingested to centralized logging pipeline (Kafka -> Splunk/Datadog/Cloud-Logging as appropriate).

Retention and retention exceptions
- Default retention (control plane): 1 year for operational logs (low-sensitivity), 3 years for admin/auth events, 7 years for compliance-critical audit trails for customers with contractual requirements.
- Sensitive data logs (PII, creds, raw customer data) must be redacted before long-term storage; raw capture only in secure staging systems with TTL <= 30 days.
- Retention exceptions: customers with stricter legal/regulatory needs may require longer retention; documented in contract and tracked in the retention register.

Integrity and tamper evidence
- All audit logs must be cryptographically signed (write-once where supported) and checksum-verified on ingestion. Any replay or gap triggers immediate investigation and an incident ticket.

Alerting and SLOs
- Logging pipeline availability SLO: 99.9% ingestion availability.
- Alert thresholds: >5% log drop rate in 5m window or >1 minute ingestion delay for error-level events triggers a P1 to SRE + Security.

3) Data Residency and Retention

Data residency principles
- Customers declare a required residency region per product agreement. Production data for that customer (model inputs, KV cache, embeddings storage, and audit records) must be stored only in the agreed region(s).
- Cross-region replication permitted only where explicitly allowed by contract; otherwise, failover must operate using regional runbooks and routing.

Retention policy (default)
- Model inputs / request payloads: default retention 30 days; can be configured to 0 days (no retention) or up to 3 years for enterprise customers with justification and legal review.
- Embeddings and derived vectors: default retention 365 days; encryption-at-rest required and access restricted to svc-owner + data-processing roles.
- Billing and metering records: minimum 7 years for financial compliance.

Data deletion and verification
- Deletion requests follow the DP-API (Data Protection API) flow: request -> validation -> scheduled deletion job -> deletion verification report generated and stored in evidence store. Retention deletion jobs are idempotent and publish a proof-of-deletion (hash) to the audit stream.

Encryption and key management
- In transit: TLS 1.2+ with strong ciphers; mutual TLS required for all inter-service control plane communication.
- At rest: AES-256 (or equivalent) with KMS-managed keys. Production customer keys use HSM-backed KMS and customer-managed keys (CMKs) where requested. Key rotation: master keys rotated annually; data-encryption keys rotated every 90 days.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Requirements by phase
- Design: Threat model required for any service handling customer data or new control-plane capabilities. Threat models include attack surface map, trust boundaries, and mitigation plan.
- Implementation: Secrets must never be committed; pre-commit hooks and CI checks (git-secrets, TruffleHog) are mandatory. Static analysis (SAST) must run on PRs for all services; block merge on critical findings.
- Testing: Dependency scanning (SCA) with automated CVE blocking policy for severity >= high; fuzzing for parsers and user-input handlers on critical services; dynamic application security testing (DAST) for public endpoints before major releases.
- Deployment: Blue/green or canary rollouts for production; automatic rollback for key errors (increased error rate, latency SLO violation, or data leakage detection).
- Release approval: Every production release touching sensitive subsystems must have sign-off from the service owner, security reviewer, and product owner.

Developer tooling and guardrails
- CI/CD: pipelines execute least-privilege deploys; production deploys require ephemeral deploy tokens and are logged to the audit stream.
- Secrets handling: Secrets stored in KMS-backed vault; access given via short-lived credentials injected by runner at build time.
- Dependency management: Approved package registries and a curated whitelist for high-risk libraries.

5) Incident Response - Security Procedures

Goals
- Contain and remediate security incidents quickly, preserve evidence for forensic analysis and compliance, and restore services while minimizing customer impact.

Triage and severity classification
- Sev-1 (Security P1): Active data exfiltration, production service compromise, customer data leakage, or cryptographic key compromise. Response: assemble IR war room (Security, SRE, Legal, CISO, Product, Exec comms). Immediate mitigation steps required within 60 minutes.
- Sev-2: Suspicious lateral movement, privilege escalation without confirmed data loss, high-severity vulnerabilities exploited in prod. Response: IR team + remediation plan within 4 hours.
- Sev-3: Low-confidence anomalies, successful exploit in non-prod, or information-only incidents. Response: investigation within 24 hours.

Preservation of evidence
- Forensic images: follow the standard forensic playbook; take snapshots of affected hosts and network captures; store on immutable evidence store with chain-of-custody metadata.
- Log preservation: freeze relevant audit logs and export to an isolated evidence bucket; generate checksums and record in the incident ticket.

Communication and regulatory obligations
- Notification windows: notify internal execs and Legal within 1 hour for Sev-1 incidents. Regulatory/customer notification timelines are handled by Legal per contract and applicable law (e.g., GDPR 72-hour window).

Post-incident
- Postmortem: written within 7 business days; include root cause, timeline, mitigations, and action items (owner + ETA). Security action items become prioritized with SRE and Engineering.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Audit preparation
- Evidence catalog: maintain a living registry of required evidence items by control (e.g., key rotation logs, access review artifacts, retention register, encryption config, incident tickets). Each evidence artifact is versioned and linked to the related control.
- Evidence owner: every control has a named owner responsible for producing evidence in the requested timeframe.

Evidence collection and storage
- Evidence store: immutable, access-logged bucket with retention aligned to the compliance need (minimum 3 years recommended). All evidence uploads must include metadata fields: control_id, owner, upload_time, and verifier.
- Automated evidence generation: where possible, outputs (access reviews, rotation runs, JIT approvals) must be emitted as machine-readable artifacts and snapshots stored automatically.

Audit response SLAs
- Internal auditor request: 5 business days for standard evidence packages.
- External SOC/ISO auditor: 10 business days unless negotiated otherwise in the audit scope.

7) Risk and Exceptions Process

Risk acceptance
- Exceptions: Temporary exceptions to controls require a documented risk assessment, compensating controls, named approver (head of security or delegated officer), and a TTL (max 90 days for high-risk exceptions). All exceptions tracked in the exception register.

Approval matrix
- Low risk: product/security team lead can approve (documentation required).
- Medium risk: Head of Security + Eng manager approval required.
- High risk (cryptography, cross-border data movement, master key handling): CISO + Legal sign-off and Exec sponsor required.

Exception review and closure
- Revalidation: all exceptions must be revalidated before TTL expiry. Any exception not remediated results in automatic escalation to the Exec security council.

Appendices

A. Useful commands and examples
- Access request (CLI example):
  curl -X POST -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" -d '{\"user\":\"alice@example.com\",\"role\":\"infra-operator\",\"ttl\":\"4h\",\"reason\":\"emergency deploy\"}' https://access.redwood.internal/api/v1/requests

- Proof-of-deletion example (DP-API response):
  {\"request_id\":\"req-20270304-abc123\", \"deleted_objects\": 42, \"deletion_hash\": \"sha256:...\"}

B. Key contacts
- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.example.com (PagerDuty)
- Incident commander escalation: ic-escalation@redwood.example.com
- Legal and privacy: legal-privacy@redwood.example.com
